opus-5.5.text:
Around 2016 to 2017, I'd say robotics was sort of split into a few camps that didn't talk to each other as much as they should have.

On one side you had the classical, model-based approach, which was really the mainstream in terms of what actually worked on real hardware. You'd have a perception pipeline that tried to estimate the state of the world, object poses, geometry, and then you'd hand that off to a motion planner or a trajectory optimizer, and then a controller would execute it. Very modular, very engineered. Task and motion planning was a big topic, people combining symbolic planners with geometric motion planning. It was principled and it worked well in structured settings, but it was brittle. If your perception was off by a centimeter, or the object wasn't in your model library, things fell apart.

Then on the other side, deep learning had just exploded in vision, and people were starting to ask, can we bring that into robotics? So you had the early end-to-end learning work, things like visuomotor policies trained directly from pixels to torques, and the large-scale grasping experiments where you'd have a bunch of robot arms collecting data in parallel. And deep reinforcement learning was very hot, mostly because of the successes in Atari and Go, so a lot of people were trying to apply RL to manipulation, often in simulation first.

But honestly, at that time the learning-based approaches were mostly demonstrated on fairly short-horizon, single-skill tasks: grasp something, push something, open a door. The question that I was really interested in was, how do you get to long-horizon tasks, things that require multiple steps and some kind of reasoning about structure, without hand-engineering everything? Because the classical folks had structure but no learning, and the learning folks had flexibility but very little structure. That gap was kind of the defining tension of that period, and a lot of my PhD work, things like neural task programming, was trying to bridge it, using imitation learning but with some compositional, hierarchical structure built into the model.

r001.rationale: The response discusses perception pipelines and deep learning in vision, but does not characterize the vision-centric approach as treating robotics itself as a computer vision problem.

r002.rationale: It says reinforcement learning interest followed successes in Atari and Go, but does not identify AlphaGo or clearly attribute the enthusiasm to AlphaGo’s success.

r003.rationale: The response describes classical methods working on real hardware and mentions parallel robot-arm data collection, but does not state that relatively little robotics research used real robots.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So if I think back to 2016, 2017, that was really the moment right after the deep learning wave had swept through computer vision, and everyone in robotics was asking, okay, can we do the same thing here? But the field was actually pretty split.

On one side you had the classical pipeline, which was still the dominant way to build a working robot. You'd have a perception module, maybe a pose estimator or an object detector, feeding into a state estimate, then a planner, then a controller. Each piece was engineered separately, often with a lot of hand-tuned heuristics, and the interfaces between them were designed by humans. That approach was reliable in structured settings, but it was brittle. Anything that violated your assumptions about the scene would break the whole chain.

On the other side you had the end-to-end learning camp, which was very exciting at the time. There was the Levine and Finn work on visuomotor policies, the Google arm farm grasping project, and a lot of enthusiasm around deep reinforcement learning after things like DQN and AlphaGo. The promise was that you'd just learn the mapping from pixels to motor commands and let the data figure out the representations. The problem was data. Deep RL needed millions of trials, and real robots are slow, expensive, and break. So most of that work either lived in simulation, or used very narrow tasks, or needed enormous hardware investments.

And then there was a smaller middle camp, which is where I found myself gravitating. People doing imitation learning and learning from demonstration, trying to get the data efficiency of having a human show the robot what to do, while still using learned representations. The questions were things like, how do you get a robot to generalize from a handful of demonstrations? How do you structure the problem so learning is tractable? That tension, between how much structure you impose and how much you let the data decide, was really the central debate, and honestly it still is, just with much larger models and much more data than we had back then.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics researchers asked whether they could apply the deep learning wave from computer vision, but it does not clearly characterize robotics as a computer vision problem.

r002.rationale: It links enthusiasm for deep reinforcement learning to developments including AlphaGo.

r003.rationale: It says much deep RL work used simulation, narrow tasks, or major hardware investments, but does not state that relatively little robotics research overall involved real robots.

astra-6.text:
Around 2016–2017, I would say the mainstream approach was still largely model-based. You would break the problem into perception, planning, and control, build each component separately, and then integrate them. A lot of the intelligence came from engineers specifying how the system should work, with fairly explicit assumptions about the robot and its environment.

At the same time, deep learning was becoming very successful in perception, and there was growing excitement about deep reinforcement learning: could a robot learn what to do through experience, instead of having every behavior engineered? So you had this established modular approach alongside an emerging push toward learning more of the system directly from data. The big challenge was getting those learning methods to work reliably on physical robots, where collecting experience is much more expensive than in simulation.

r001.rationale: The response describes a modular, model-based approach and growing interest in learning, but does not characterize vision-centric robotics as treating robotics as a computer vision problem.

r002.rationale: It mentions growing excitement about deep reinforcement learning, but does not attribute that enthusiasm to AlphaGo’s success.

r003.rationale: It says experience on physical robots was expensive, but does not state that relatively little robotics research involved real robots.

sol-6.1.text:
Around 2016–2017, I would say there were two main approaches. One was the more classical robotics approach: you build a model of the world, break the problem into perception, planning, and control, and engineer each component. That can work very well when the environment is structured and you understand the task.

The other was learning-based robotics, where you try to learn behavior from data, through reinforcement learning or demonstrations. Deep learning was making a big impact on perception, and people were exploring whether that success could extend to robot actions. The challenge was that robots need to interact with the physical world, so collecting data and learning through trial and error were much harder than working with images on a computer.

r001.rationale: It says deep learning was influencing perception and mentions attempts to extend that success to robot actions, but does not characterize the vision-centric approach as treating robotics as a computer vision problem.

r002.rationale: It mentions reinforcement learning but does not connect interest in it to AlphaGo’s success.

r003.rationale: It says real-world robot data collection and trial-and-error learning were difficult, but does not state that relatively little research used real robots.
